Lying can be defined as ‘intentionally communicating a falsehood to another person’ (p. 10). This definition is problematic in the context of caring for people with dementia for two reasons. First, intention is difficult to ascertain and, second, the meaning of ‘truth’ is ambiguous. ## 1. Introduction

Lying is a topic that fascinates people, as evidenced by the number of books that have been written on the subject (e.g., Kipnis, 2006; McGehee, 2006; Sissela Bok, 1978/2002; Tavris & Aronson, 2007). In this paper, we report the results of a Delphi study that aimed to reach consensus on a definition of lying. This is important because there is no agreement on what constitutes lying, which has implications for research and practice. For example, a lack of agreement may hinder the development of a taxonomy of deception, which in turn hinders empirical investigations of lying and deceit. In addition, the inability to agree on a definition of lying makes it difficult to determine the prevalence of lying in society and the extent to which lying is a socially adaptive behavior.

Participants receive feedback on responses to previous rounds and can use this feedback to inform their decisions about future survey responses and the process continues until there is emergence of consensus (Gordon & Pease 2006; Vernon 2009). Delphi studies commonly comprise three rounds before consensus is achieved (Hasson et al. 2000; Hanafin & Brooks 2005). The Delphi method consists of three rounds of questionnaires that solicit participants’ opinions on a topic of interest. Participants are recruited from a pool of stakeholders who have a vested interest in the topic, such as clinicians, administrators, policy makers, etc. In round one, participants are asked to respond to open-ended questions, which are used to generate a list of issues related to the topic. In round two, participants are asked to rate the importance of each issue on a Likert scale from 1 (not important) to 5 (extremely important). The results of this round are summarized and presented to participants in round three, along with a request for feedback on the summary. Participants are given the opportunity to revise their ratings based on the feedback and new information provided in the summary. The goal of the Delphi method is to achieve consensus on the most important issues related to the topic under study.</s>

This article explores the ethics of therapeutic lying in dementia care and provides guidance for practitioners who wish to engage in therapeutic lying.

Therapeutic lying has been practiced for thousands of years by physicians, psychologists, social workers, clergy and other caregivers in an attempt to relieve suffering and promote well-being. It is a form of deceit that is intended to help people cope with reality by altering it in some way. In the case of dementia, therapeutic lying may be used to protect the person’s self-esteem, avoid anxiety, maintain social relationships, and/or reduce feelings of loneliness and abandonment.

There are a number of situations in which therapeutic lying may be appropriate:

They viewed themselves as the representatives of the person with dementia in the later stages because they knew them, knew their life history and knew what mattered to them. At the heart of informal/unpaid carers actions was the intention to benefit the person with dementia and they reported that therapeutic lying was appropriate when it benefited and respected the person's dignity. A few informal/unpaid carers in the current study reported that they sometimes felt uncomfortable 'lying' to the person with dementia as it might increase the person with dementia's confusion or negatively impact on their relationship. Life was fragile and its continued existence required treading the fine line marking the boundary between those circumstances necessary to maintain it, and those circumstances sufficient to extinguish it. Where the environment alone did not guarantee that line could be held, intelligence arose to force it actively, and the more delicate and complex the balancing act became, the more intelligence evolved to sustain it. ## 1 Samuel 15:10-11

10 And the word of the LORD came to Samuel, saying, 11 I repent that I have set up Saul to be king: for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments. And it grieved Samuel; and he cried unto the LORD all night.

Samuel's sorrow was for Saul, but God's sorrow was for Himself. The word "repent" is used in the Hebrew to mean "to change one's mind" and that is what God did in this case. He changed His mind about Saul as king over Israel.

Saul was the first king of Israel and his reign was marked by disobedience to God from the outset. In spite of this, God continued to give him chance after chance to get his life right with God. But Saul never took advantage of these gracious opportunities, and God finally had to take drastic action to deal with Saul's stubborn refusal to obey Him.
